  ]
}

Note: Here as well similar mapping happens to Errorcode and ErrorMsg fields, so im not pasting debug screenshots again. Please refer to Projection/BS1 layer for the same. 

Response:

  • From above screenshot, it's evident that BS-2 is executed sucessfully and response log gets mapped to renamed fields Errorcode and ErrorMsg.

Limitations:

  • Only RAP Normal Deep Actions supported here and static and instance RAP Actions are strictly not supported since it cant be redefined. 
  • This redefinition will work only for Deep Actions with OData V4. For Normal Action without Deep syntax, it will not work. (Note: Regarding RAP Deep Actions and OData V4, I have already explained in my earlier blog - RAP - Deep Static Action with OData V4 ). 
  • Keyword SUB is not supported in RAP Actions without the term corresponding in it. If we use it directly then for some of the SAP patch level, using a=sub combined with hierarchy mapping caused a hard SYSTEM_CORE_DUMPED (Signal 11) in the ABAP Kernel during ADT activation as below.

  • To avoid the kernel crash, I avoided the usage of syntax SUB Directly and relied on SUB with CORRESPONDING as below. 
deep mapping for ya_material_api_parameter corresponding  {
      Id      = Id;
      Product = Product;
      AckCode = AckCode;
      Status  = Status;
      sub _MaterialData = _MaterialData;
      sub _log = _log;
    }
  • Instead of using Behaviour Projection in higher layers, If we use Behaviour Interface it doesnt intent to support even in RAP V4. It gives error in Service as below. (i..e to enable Behaviour Interface, we must add provider contract transactional_interface at Projection layer ). 
  • Cardinality is not supported in Deep Result at Projection/Interface levels. The cardinality given in base layer is directly applicable to all the redefinitions. 

  • Since Abstract Entities are action parameter and they wont directly refer to standard structures/cds views, henceforth manual field mapping should be done. 

CONCLUSION:

Henceforth, in this way RAP Action Parameter Redefinition is used to decouple Material Master API at base and projection layer. Not only Material Master API for interface, but also this approach can use used for Fiori app integrations as well based on the requirement. Moreover, I can say this is a very good feature given by RAP to use Mandatory Action Parameter based on business requirement. This makes the backend highly reusable and reliable.  Also, OData V4 on top of this makes the metadata lighter and powerful.

entry.title: Clean Core After Go-Live: A Step-by-Step Analysis — and Why You Must Repeat It Periodically
entry.content:
A quick word on what we’re measuring

Clean Core scoring grades your custom code on three ATC checks — Usage of APIs, Allowed enhancement technologies, and Customer modifications — and assigns each object a level from A to D. The level is simply the highest ATC priority the object triggers (P1 → D, P2 → C, P3 → B). Level A is fully clean; Level D needs redesign. Keep that A–D idea in mind — we’ll come back to it.

Part 1 — How I ran the Clean Core analysis

Step 1.  Prerequisites (OSS Notes) — before running anything, get two SAP Notes in place. SAP Note 3781180 explains how to get the latest released-API list (the classification content behind the checks). SAP Note 3752345 enables ATC Quick Fixes, so you can later swap objects to released successors mechanically. Also confirm the ATC content/variant note that applies to your specific release.

Step 2.  Set up the Clean Core check variant — configure the ABAP Cloud / clean-core readiness check variant in ATC. The key check is "Usage of Released APIs (Cloudification Repository)", alongside the allowed-enhancement-technologies and customer-modification checks. This variant is what turns a raw code base into A–D findings.

Step 3.  Load the classification (the program) — run report SYCM_API_CLASSIFICATION_MANAGR. This loads SAP’s cloudification classification (the released / deprecated API data) into your system, and it is also where you generate or adjust your own partner JSON for your custom and classic APIs. This step is easy to miss — skip it and you score against stale data.

Step 4.  Run the analysis — you have two routes. ATC in ADT / SE80 is best for developers who want to drill into findings object by object. The Custom Code Migration (CCM) Fiori app is best for a consolidated, project-level view — and it’s where you’ll import usage data later. Run against your custom (Z/Y) packages.

Step 5.  Read the levels — SAP publishes the classification openly in the cloudification repository (github.com/SAP/abap-atc-cr-cv-s4hc). This is where each object maps to a Level A–D and, where one exists, its released successor. Sort findings by level: fix D first, plan C, and treat B (classic APIs with no successor) as "keep and wrap".

 

 

Step 6.  Overlay real usage (SUSG) — ATC tells you what isn’t clean; usage tells you what still matters. Activate SCMON in your production system, let it run a representative window, aggregate with transaction SUSG, create a snapshot, and import it into the CCM app. Your "redesign" pile now splits in two: decommission (unused code — just switch it off) and redesign (used code — actually remediate). Decommissioning unused code is the fastest, lowest-risk way to shrink scope.

That completes the one-time Clean Core / ATC baseline.

A note on Z-fields — coming soon.  Many of you will have a lot of Z-fields that came across from ECC to S/4HANA and were added as custom SE11 append fields. With SAP ABAP-Managed Fields (AMF), you can now make these fields available in Fiori apps, CDS views, and analytics — without recreating them and preserving the history(data), I’ll cover this in more detail in a follow-up blog.

Part 2 — Why (and how) to check it periodically

Here’s the part most teams miss. A Clean Core score is not a constant — it drifts:

  • SAP keeps releasing new APIs, so yesterday’s "no successor" becomes today’s quick fix.
  • Your team keeps writing custom code, adding new findings.
  • Usage changes — code goes cold and should be decommissioned, not remediated.

A number from six months ago tells you where you were, not where you are. So I treat Clean Core as a recurring check, with this simple loop:

  1. Run a fresh ATC — as a gate on every transport, plus a scheduled quarterly full run.
  2. Refresh the repo first — re-pull the latest cloudification JSON (re-run SYCM_API_CLASSIFICATION_MANAGR) before each run, or you’ll score against an old API list.
  3. Upload the ATC results to SAP Readiness Check — to see custom-code readiness in context.
  4. Trend it in SAP Cloud ALM — the Clean Core dashboard on the RISE with SAP Methodology Dashboard turns each run into a curve leadership can act on.

 

Wrapping up

Clean Core is a ongoing process and should not be treated as a one time activity. Run the analysis once to get your baseline — then refresh the yardstick, re-score against real usage, and trend the result on a cadence. Do that, and every future build sits on a core that is getting cleaner, not drifting.

How often does your team re-check? I’d love to hear your cadence in the comments.

References

  • Clean Core – Part 1: Activation of the RISE with SAP Methodology Dashboard on SAP Cloud ALM (SAP Community): https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/clean-core-part-1-activation-of-rise-with-sap-methodology-dashboard-on/ba-p/14328522
  • ABAP Test Cockpit (ATC) recommendations for governance of clean core ABAP development (SAP Community): https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/abap-test-cockpit-atc-recommendations-for-governance-of-clean-core-abap/ba-p/14186130
  • SAP Cloudification Repository (released / classic API list): https://github.com/SAP/abap-atc-cr-cv-s4hc
  • SAP Note 3781180 (getting the latest released-API list)  ·  SAP Note 3752345 (enable ATC Quick Fixes)

entry.title: SAP RAP Deep Dive: Demystifying %is_draft During Instance Creation
entry.content:
Introduction

The ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) provides a built-in draft mechanism that allows users to work with business data before it becomes active.

In a draft-enabled RAP Business Object, an instance can exist in two different transactional states:

  • Active instance – the business data has been activated and belongs to the active persistence.
  • Draft instance – the business data is currently being created or edited and has not yet been activated.

When a RAP application is consumed through Fiori Elements, most of the draft processing is handled automatically by the RAP framework.

However, the situation becomes more interesting when we work directly with EML (Entity Manipulation Language).

While implementing actions, reads, creates, determinations, validations, or other behavior logic, we may encounter a special component called: %is_draft

This component is part of the BDEF-derived types used by RAP and helps identify whether a transactional instance represents a draft or an active instance.

In this blog, we will understand the role of %is_draft, its relationship with %tky, and how draft and active instances are addressed while working with EML.

1. What is %is_draft?

%is_draft is a technical component provided by the RAP framework for draft-enabled Business Objects.

Its primary purpose is to indicate whether the transactional instance being addressed is a draft or an active instance.

The two possible values are:

if_abap_behv=>mk-on

and

if_abap_behv=>mk-off

Conceptually:

%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
                     |
                     v
                Draft Instance


%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-off
                     |
                     v
                Active Instance

 Therefore, whenever we see %is_draft in an EML structure, we should think of it as the technical indicator that helps RAP distinguish between the draft and active transactional instances.

2. Why Do We Need %is_draft?

Consider a Billing Document with the following business key:

Billing Document = 1000000001

In a draft-enabled RAP Business Object, the framework can have an active version and a draft version associated with the same business object.

Conceptually:

                 Billing Document
                    1000000001
                         |
              +----------+----------+
              |                     |
              v                     v
           Active                  Draft
           Instance                Instance

The business key alone is not sufficient to describe the complete transactional identity.

RAP therefore needs additional information to determine which version of the instance is being addressed.

This is where %is_draft becomes important.

3. %is_draft and %tky

One of the most important concepts to understand is the relationship between %is_draft and %tky.

For a draft-enabled Business Object, %tky represents the transactional key.

The transactional key contains the business key together with the draft information.

For example, conceptually:

%tky
 |
 +-- Business Key
 |
 +-- %is_draft

Therefore, %tky allows RAP to distinguish between:

1000000001 + Active

and:

1000000001 + Draft

This is why %tky is commonly used in RAP behavior implementations when referring to instances.

For example:

%tky = VALUE #(
  %key-BillId = '1000000001'
  %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
)

Here, the transactional key identifies the draft version of the Billing Document.

4. A Simple Billing Document Scenario

Let's use a simple Billing Document Business Object throughout this example.

Assume we have the following entity:

ZBR_T_BILL_HEADER

with fields such as:

BillId
BillDate
BillType
Currency
CustomerId
NetAmount
SalesOrg

The Business Object is draft-enabled.

We want to implement an action called:

copyBillingDocument

The requirement is:

Copy an existing Billing Document and create a new Billing Document while allowing the caller to specify the required draft context.

The basic process is:

Existing Billing Document
            |
            |
            | copyBillingDocument
            |
            v
    New Billing Document

 

5. Creating a Draft Instance Using EML

Let's first look at a simple CREATE operation.

When the EML request contains:

%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-on

the request identifies the instance as a draft instance.

Example:

MODIFY ENTITIES OF zbrt_i_bill_header
  ENTITY zbrt_i_bill_header
  CREATE FIELDS
    (
      BillId
      BillDate
      BillType
      Currency
      CustomerId
      NetAmount
      SalesOrg
    )
    WITH VALUE #(
      (
        %is_draft  = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
        BillId     = '1000000005'
        BillDate   = cl_abap_context_info=>get_system_date( )
        BillType   = 'F2'
        Currency   = 'INR'
        CustomerId = '100001'
        NetAmount  = '5000'
        SalesOrg   = '1000'
      )
    )
    MAPPED DATA(mapped)
    FAILED DATA(failed)
    REPORTED DATA(reported).

 The important part is:

%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-on

This indicates the draft context for the create request.

6. Identifying an Active Instance

Now consider an active instance.

The draft indicator is:

%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-off

For example:

%tky = VALUE #(
  %key-BillId = '1000000001'
  %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-off
)

This identifies the active transactional instance.

Therefore:

%is_draft = ON
       |
       +---- Draft


%is_draft = OFF
       |
       +---- Active

7. Implementing the Copy Action

Now let's move to a more realistic scenario.

We create an action:

copyBillingDocument

The action receives the source Billing Document and a parameter indicating the requested draft state for the newly created document.

The action implementation reads the source instance and prepares the data for a new instance.

Example implementation:

METHOD copyBillingDocument.

  DATA:
    lt_billingdocuments TYPE TABLE FOR CREATE
                         zbrt_i_bill_header\zbrt_i_bill_header,
    lv_billingdoc       TYPE c LENGTH 10.

  "Get the highest existing Billing Document number
  SELECT FROM zbrt_i_bill_header
    FIELDS MAX( BillId )
    INTO @lv_billingdoc.

  "Generate the next Billing Document number
  lv_billingdoc = lv_billingdoc + 1.

  "Read the source Billing Document
  READ ENTITIES OF zbrt_i_bill_header IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY zbrt_i_bill_header
    ALL FIELDS WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_billdoc).

  LOOP AT lt_billdoc ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_billdoc>).

    APPEND VALUE #(

      %cid = keys[
               KEY entity
               %key = <ls_billdoc>-%key
             ]-%cid

      %is_draft = keys[
                    KEY entity
                    %key = <ls_billdoc>-%key
                  ]-%param-%is_draft

      %data = CORRESPONDING #(
                <ls_billdoc>
                EXCEPT BillId )

    )
    TO lt_billingdocuments
    ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_new_bill>).

    "Set new Billing Document number
    <ls_new_bill>-BillId =
      CONV #( lv_billingdoc ).

    "Set new Billing Date
    <ls_new_bill>-BillDate =
      cl_abap_context_info=>get_system_date( ).

  ENDLOOP.

  "Create the new Billing Document
  MODIFY ENTITIES OF zbrt_i_bill_header IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY zbrt_i_bill_header
    CREATE
    FIELDS
      (
        BillId
        BillDate
        BillType
        Currency
        CustomerId
        NetAmount
        SalesOrg
      )
    WITH lt_billingdocuments
    MAPPED DATA(mapped_create).

  "Return created instances
  mapped-zbrt_i_bill_header =
    mapped_create-zbrt_i_bill_header.

ENDMETHOD.

8. Understanding the Important Line

The most important line in the above implementation is:

%is_draft = keys[
                KEY entity
                %key = <ls_billdoc>-%key
              ]-%param-%is_draft

Let's break it down.

The action receives the requested draft state through:

%param-%is_draft

The implementation then forwards this value to the CREATE request:

%is_draft

So the flow is:

Action Parameter
      |
      v
%param-%is_draft
      |
      v
Create Structure
      |
      v
%is_draft
      |
      v
RAP Runtime

This allows the action implementation to pass the requested draft context to the subsequent EML CREATE operation.

9. Executing the Action Using EML

To test the action, we can create an ABAP class implementing:

IF_OO_ADT_CLASSRUN

and execute the EML from the class.

The action can be called like this:

MODIFY ENTITIES OF zbrt_i_bill_header
  ENTITY zbrt_i_bill_header
  EXECUTE copyBillingDocument
  FROM VALUE #(
    (
      %cid = 'COPY_001'

      %tky = VALUE #(
        %key-BillId = '1000000001'
        %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-off
      )

      %param-%is_draft =
        if_abap_behv=>mk-on
    )
  )
  MAPPED DATA(mapped)
  FAILED DATA(failed)
  REPORTED DATA(reported).

Here:

%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-off

inside %tky identifies the source instance as active.

And:

%param-%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-on

passes the requested draft state to the action.

Conceptually:

Source
Active
  |
  |
  | copyBillingDocument
  |
  v
New Instance
Draft

10. Scenario: Draft Source

Now consider that the source Billing Document itself is a draft.

The transactional key should identify the draft instance:

%tky = VALUE #(
  %key-BillId = '1000000002'
  %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
)

For example:

MODIFY ENTITIES OF zbrt_i_bill_header
  ENTITY zbrt_i_bill_header
  EXECUTE copyBillingDocument
  FROM VALUE #(
    (
      %cid = 'COPY_002'

      %tky = VALUE #(
        %key-BillId = '1000000002'
        %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
      )

      %param-%is_draft =
        if_abap_behv=>mk-on
    )
  )
  MAPPED DATA(mapped)
  FAILED DATA(failed)
  REPORTED DATA(reported).

Here the source transactional instance is a draft.

The requested target context is also draft.

The conceptual flow is:

Draft Source
     |
     |
     | copyBillingDocument
     |
     v
Draft Target

11. Understanding the Difference Between Source and Target

This is an important point when working with actions.

There are two different questions:

Question 1: Which instance should the action operate on?

This is determined by the transactional key:

%tky

which contains the instance key and draft information.

Question 2: What should happen to the newly created instance?

This is controlled by the data passed to the CREATE operation, including the draft context where applicable.

Therefore, we should not confuse:

%tky-%is_draft

with:

%param-%is_draft

They can represent different parts of the operation.

Conceptually:

                 Action
                   |
          +--------+--------+
          |                 |
          v                 v
     Source State       Target State
          |                 |
       %tky              CREATE
          |                 |
     %is_draft          %is_draft

This distinction is particularly useful in copy-by-action scenarios.

12. Active Source and Draft Target

Let's take another example.

Suppose:

Source Billing Document
BillId = 1000000001
State  = Active

We execute:

%tky = VALUE #(
  %key-BillId = '1000000001'
  %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-off
)

and request:

%param-%is_draft =
  if_abap_behv=>mk-on

The conceptual flow is:

             Active
               |
               |
               | Action
               |
               v
             Draft

The source and target therefore have different transactional states.

13. Draft Source and Draft Target

Now consider:

Source = Draft
Target = Draft

The source key is:

%tky = VALUE #(
  %key-BillId = '1000000002'
  %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-on
)

and the requested target context is:

%param-%is_draft =
  if_abap_behv=>mk-on

Conceptually:

             Draft
               |
               |
               | Action
               |
               v
             Draft

14. Active Source and Active Target

The same concept can be applied when both the source and target are active.

The source transactional key would identify the active instance:

%tky = VALUE #(
  %key-BillId = '1000000001'
  %is_draft   = if_abap_behv=>mk-off
)

and the requested target context would be active:

%param-%is_draft =
  if_abap_behv=>mk-off

Conceptually:

             Active
                |
                |
                | Action
                |
                v
             Active

The important point is that the source and target contexts are separate considerations.

15. Scenario Summary

The different combinations can be summarized as follows:

Source State Target State Source %is_draft Target %is_draft
ActiveActiveOFFOFF
ActiveDraftOFFON
DraftDraftONON
DraftActiveONOFF

This table is useful when debugging EML requests involving draft-enabled Business Objects.

16. Using %tky in Behavior Implementations

When implementing RAP behavior methods, we frequently receive keys in the keys parameter.

For example:

METHOD someAction.

  READ ENTITIES OF zbrt_i_bill_header IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY zbrt_i_bill_header
    ALL FIELDS WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_billdoc).

ENDMETHOD.

The keys passed to the method represent the transactional instances on which the operation is being performed.

For draft-enabled objects, %tky carries the required draft information.

Therefore, developers should avoid unnecessarily reconstructing the transactional identity manually.

Using the RAP-generated key structures helps the implementation remain aligned with the framework's draft handling.

17. Draft Handling Through Fiori Elements

When a draft-enabled RAP Business Object is consumed through Fiori Elements, developers normally do not have to manually set %is_draft.

For example, the user might perform:

Create
  |
  v
Draft
  |
  v
Edit Data
  |
  v
Save
  |
  v
Activate
  |
  v
Active

The RAP framework manages the corresponding draft lifecycle.

The developer mainly needs to understand %is_draft when working with lower-level RAP operations such as:

  • EML
  • Behavior implementations
  • Actions
  • Determinations
  • Validations
  • Custom transactional logic

18. Important Difference Between Draft State and Activation

One important point should be kept in mind.

%is_draft indicates the draft context of an instance involved in a transactional operation.

It should not be treated as a replacement for the complete RAP draft lifecycle.

For example:

Draft
  |
  | Activate
  v
Active

Activation is a RAP draft lifecycle operation.

Simply thinking of activation as:

%is_draft = if_abap_behv=>mk-off

does not by itself represent the complete activation process.

The RAP framework performs the required processing for the transition between draft and active states.

Therefore, %is_draft should be understood as an instance-state indicator, not as an instruction to manually move data between draft and active persistence.

19. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Treating %is_draft as an Application Field

%is_draft is not a normal business field such as:

BillId
Customer
Currency
Amount

It is a technical component generated by RAP for transactional processing.

Mistake 2: Using Only the Business Key

For a draft-enabled object, the application key alone may not be enough to describe the transactional instance.

For example:

BillId = 1000000001

does not by itself communicate whether the request refers to the draft or active version.

The transactional key carries this information.

Mistake 3: Confusing %key and %tky

%key represents the business key.

%tky represents the transactional key.

For draft-enabled objects, %tky also contains the draft information.

Conceptually:

%key
 |
 +-- Business Key


%tky
 |
 +-- Business Key
 |
 +-- Draft Information

Mistake 4: Assuming the UI Requires Manual Draft Handling

In a normal Fiori Elements application, the RAP framework handles most draft processing automatically.

Manual handling becomes relevant mainly when implementing custom EML or behavior logic.

Mistake 5: Directly Manipulating Draft Persistence

The draft persistence is managed by the RAP framework.

Application logic should use RAP behavior and EML rather than directly inserting, updating, or deleting records in the draft table.

20. A Simple Mental Model

The easiest way to remember %is_draft is:

                    RAP Transaction
                          |
                 +--------+--------+
                 |                 |
                 v                 v
              Active             Draft
                 |                 |
                 v                 v
           %is_draft OFF      %is_draft ON

And when we use %tky:

                    %tky
                      |
             +--------+--------+
             |                 |
          Business Key      %is_draft

Therefore, whenever you see:

%tky

in a draft-enabled RAP Business Object, remember that the transactional identity also carries the information required to distinguish the draft and active instance.

21. Key Takeaways

The most important points from this article are:

1. %is_draft is a RAP technical indicator

It identifies the draft context of a transactional instance.

2. ON represents draft and OFF represents active

if_abap_behv=>mk-on

represents the draft context, while:

if_abap_behv=>mk-off

represents the active context.

3. %is_draft is related to %tky

For draft-enabled Business Objects, the transactional key contains the draft information.

4. %tky is important in behavior implementations

It helps the RAP runtime identify the correct transactional instance.

5. Actions can operate on draft or active instances

The transactional key determines the source instance being addressed.

6. Source and target state are separate concepts

In a copy/create-by-action scenario, the source can be active while the target is draft, or both can be draft, depending on the implementation and RAP lifecycle rules.

7. Fiori Elements hides much of this complexity

When using standard draft-enabled Fiori Elements applications, RAP manages most of the draft lifecycle automatically.

8. %is_draft is not the same as activation

It identifies the transactional state; it should not be considered a replacement for RAP's draft activation lifecycle.

Conclusion

Draft handling is one of the powerful features of SAP RAP, but it can initially be confusing when we start working with EML and behavior implementations.

The %is_draft component provides an important piece of information to the RAP runtime by distinguishing draft and active transactional instances.

The relationship can be remembered as:

                 Draft-enabled RAP BO
                         |
                         v
                       %tky
                         |
                +--------+--------+
                |                 |
             %is_draft        Business Key
                |
          +-----+-----+
          |           |
         ON          OFF
          |           |
        Draft       Active

Once this relationship is clear, it becomes much easier to understand why %tky is used extensively in RAP behavior implementations and how EML identifies the correct transactional instance.

Rather than thinking of %is_draft as just a simple Boolean flag, it is better to view it as part of RAP's transactional identity and draft-processing mechanism.

That understanding becomes especially valuable when implementing custom actions, EML-based operations, determinations, validations, and other advanced RAP scenarios.

entry.title: sap-harness Series (2) — How the ADT mirror works
entry.content:
Disclaimer: This is a personal blog post about a personal side project. The views here are my own, not an official SAP or employer position.

Introduction. This is Part 2 of a series on sap-harness, a tool that mirrors SAP ABAP Cloud / RAP objects to real local files so CLI coding agents like Claude Code can read and edit them directly. Part 1 explained why that mirror has to exist; this post gets into the mechanics of it — the actual SAP ADT REST API calls sap:sync and sap:push make, in the order they have to happen in, and the mistakes that order came from.

TL;DR: Part 1 covered the why (a virtual filesystem is a dealbreaker for CLI agents); this one covers the how. Walking a package, reading source, writing it back, checking for drift — every one of those steps against the ADT REST API took at least one live mistake to get right: a guessed URI, a lock released in the wrong order, a 200 that was not actually a success. This post is those mistakes and the protocol details that came out of fixing them. Verified against a live SAP BTP ABAP Cloud / S/4HANA Cloud system — a classic on-premise NetWeaver system may answer some of these differently, and where I know of a difference I say so.

Quick orientation if you have not read Part 1: sap:sync pulls SAP objects into local files (the “mirror”), sap:push uploads and activates local changes, sap:status checks the two against each other without calling SAP. All three are CLI commands (npm run sap:*) sap-harness adds on top of a normal Node project.

Planned series:

  1. Why I built sap-harness (published)
  2. How the ADT mirror works — what sap:sync / sap:push exchange with the SAP ADT REST API (this post)
  3. The story of building this tool itself with an AI agent — commits, days, and the rules that kept it honest
  4. Hands-on with the CLI + VS Code extension, and what still doesn't work

Table of Contents

  1. Walking the package tree
  2. Reading source: let the server tell you where things live
  3. Writing back: lock, push, unlock — and only then activate
  4. A 200 response is not the same thing as success
  5. Local drift, without touching the server
  6. What's next

1. Walking the Package Tree

sap:sync starts by asking SAP one question: what's inside this package? The answer comes from:

POST /sap/bc/adt/repository/nodestructure?parent_type=DEVC/K&parent_name=<PACKAGE>

POST, not GET — a GET to the same URL returns a flat 405, which is exactly the kind of detail you only learn by trying it once. The response wraps the object list in <asx:abap>, and each child comes back as a SEU_ADT_REPOSITORY_OBJ_NODE element — not as attributes on a parent tag the way a lot of other ADT responses are shaped. Parse for the wrong shape and you get an empty list, not an error, which is worse.

One thing this post assumes throughout and never re-explains per request: every call below needs a stateful session and a valid X-CSRF-Token (fetched separately, then sent on every POST/PUT), plus whatever BTP ABAP Cloud authentication got you there in the first place. Follow these URIs cold and the first one will 403 on the token, not on anything below.

Packages nest, and nodestructure doesn't hand you the chain to the top. To resolve a package's parent you call GET /sap/bc/adt/packages/<name> separately and read pak:superPackage off the response, one hop at a time, until you hit a package with none. I walked a four-level-deep package chain this way, once — I have not found a shortcut endpoint that returns the whole ancestry in one call, but I also have not gone looking very hard (the object-search and where-used endpoints under informationsystem/ answer different questions, not this one).

2. Reading Source: Let the Server Tell You Where Things Live

Once sap-harness knows an object exists, it needs the object's own URI from the server response — not a URI it guessed from the object type. This mattered more than I expected.

Most objects serve their source from <object-uri>/source/main. Reasonable assumption: CDS view definitions ought to live under something like /sap/bc/adt/ddic/cds/sources/. That assumption is wrong — the real path is /sap/bc/adt/ddic/ddl/sources/, and the cds guess just 404s. Tables and structures (TABL/DT, TABL/DS) both turn out to serve their DDL through the same /source/main pattern too, which contradicted an earlier note in this repo's own docs claiming tables had no source resource at all — wrong, and now corrected after checking it against a live system.

A handful of object types don't follow the /source/main pattern at all: service bindings (SRVB/SVB), data elements (DTEL/DE), domains (DOMA/DD), enhancement spots (ENHS/XS). For those, the bare object URI itself returns an XML document — there's no separate source child resource to ask for. Hardcode the pattern and you'll get a 404 on exactly the object types where you'd least expect it.

The rule that survived: never build a source URI from the object type. Always follow the URI the server handed you in the nodestructure or discovery response.

3. Writing Back: Lock, Push, Unlock — and Only Then Activate

The write path is LOCK → PUT → UNLOCK → ACTIVATE, one lock/unlock pair per object, with activation batched once at the end of a run across everything that changed.

I had this in the wrong order for a while: activate before unlock. It looked reasonable — you just modified the object, so activate it while you still hold the lock, then let go. SAP disagreed: with the lock still held, activation comes back 403, because as far as the server is concerned the object is still being edited by someone. --activate never once succeeded until I moved UNLOCK ahead of ACTIVATE in the sequence. It's the kind of ordering bug that's invisible in the code — both calls are there, they're just in an order that happens to be wrong every single time. (It is not a session problem in disguise, in case you are wondering the way I did: the vendor tooling this harness learned the sequence from runs an integration test that unlocks, activates, and then re-locks the very same object in the very same stateful session — proof that only the lock has to go, not the session.)

Activation itself is one call for the whole batch:

POST /sap/bc/adt/activation?method=activate&preauditRequested=true

with a body listing every changed object as <adtcore:objectReferences>. Drop the method=activate query parameter and the same endpoint returns 400 instead of doing anything useful with the body. preauditRequested=true rides along on every call too — it is required by the vendor tooling this was learned from, and I do not actually know what it changes; nothing I have read documents it either.

Content-Type on the PUT itself isn't fixed either — it depends on what's in the body. An XML prolog means application/*; anything else is text/plain; charset=utf-8. Before I made that distinction, everything went out as application/octet-stream, which SAP was fine with for most objects and flatly rejected with 415 for behavior definitions (.bdef).

4. A 200 Response Is Not the Same Thing as Success

This is the one that cost the most debugging time, and it turned out to need more than one signal, not less. The activation endpoint returns 200 whether the activation actually succeeded or not — success and failure look identical at the HTTP layer, the difference is inside the body.

The first signal is chkl:properties's own activationExecuted attribute: "false" is SAP stating outright that nothing activated, even when no message says so. But it is not sufficient on its own either way — on one run that SAP actually refused, activationExecuted still came back "true". So a false reading is trusted; a true reading is checked further, against a separate list of objects SAP reports as still inactive, and against chkl:msg entries typed E, A, or X (warnings — W — and info messages — I — do not block it). Only when none of those three say otherwise does this count as a success. A response carrying just chkl:properties and nothing else — no messages, no inactive-objects list — is what a clean activation actually looks like, but treat that shape itself as the proof and you have re-implemented the bug in a quieter font: check what is not there for the wrong reason and a future response with a new field you did not anticipate reads as failure, or worse, a refusal with a truthful activationExecuted="false" and nothing else reads as success.

5. Local Drift, Without Touching the Server

Every mirrored file carries an embedded header — @​SAP-METADATA-START through @​SAP-METADATA-END — with the package, object type and name, the object's ADT URI, a content_hash, a state (only two values exist: empty, or inactive), and when it was last synced. The comment syntax adapts to the file so nothing stops compiling: /* */ for CDS, "* for ABAP, <!-- --> for XML-shaped objects. The hash is a plain SHA-256 over the source text alone, after normalizing line endings and trimming — the header itself is stripped out first, on both sides: sap:push uploads the bare source, header excluded, and the hash is computed the same way, or the file would never match itself.

sap:status reads this and nothing else. No request goes to SAP. It strips the header, re-hashes the remaining body, compares that against the hash the header recorded, and sorts the result into NEW (no header yet), MODIFIED (hash mismatch), or UNCHANGED (hash matches). It separately tracks whether an object pushed cleanly but never got confirmed active — from the header's state field and a small pending-retry queue on disk — so a file that is byte-for-byte UNCHANGED can still be flagged as inactive on the server. Bytes and activation state are tracked as two different questions, on purpose, because they can disagree. What this does not catch: a colleague editing the same object in Eclipse. sap:status only ever compares your local file to your own last sync — there is no ETag or server-side check on push, so two people editing the same object is a race with no referee, same as it would be without any of this tooling.

One sharp edge here, fixed recently: --prune deletes local package directories SAP no longer accounts for, but used to leave their now-empty parent directories behind forever — a stale marker holding nothing, never exercised by any test until someone actually repointed a tenant at a different package tree and pruned.

Each object gets its own lock handle — the actual call is POST <OBJECT_URI>?_action=LOCK; acquireObjectLock is just this harness's own function name for that call, not a wire term. So pushing several objects in one run is several independent LOCK/PUT/UNLOCK cycles, not one lock held over the whole batch. But the lock still lives inside the session that took it out: kill the session and the lock goes with it, same as it would for a single object. What this harness does handle: a lock that gets stranded mid-push (the process dies, the network drops) is recorded and cleared on the next sap:push --retry. What it does not handle yet: any backoff or batching logic if SAP starts throttling a large push — that path is unexercised, and I am not going to describe behavior I have not seen.

The same local mirror, browsable in VS Code's Package Explorer — everything sap:sync pulled down, no live connection required to look at it.

What this buys, concretely: an agent asked to fix a CDS view does grep -rl ZI_LDG_FLIGHT abap/, opens the one real file that comes back, edits the as select from clause, and hands off to npm run sap:push -- --activate. No IDE extension API in the loop, no object browsed one click at a time — the same three or four shell commands a script or a human would run.

Conclusion

Walking the package tree, reading source without guessing at its URI, writing back in the order SAP actually accepts, and treating a 200 as a shape to parse rather than an answer to trust — that is the whole mechanism behind sap:sync and sap:push. None of it is exotic; all of it took a live mistake to get right the first time. The rules that survived, if you want them without the stories: never build a source URI from the object type, always follow the one the server gave you. Unlock before you activate, not after. A 200 from /activation is a shape you parse, not an answer you trust. Hash the body, never the file with its own header still attached. And check the drift you can — local, byte-for-byte — honestly, so you know exactly what it does not cover.

6. What's Next

None of this — the node walk, the write sequence, the drift check — needed an AI agent in the loop. It's the boring, load-bearing plumbing underneath the part I actually want to write about next: what it was like handing the building of this tool to an AI coding agent, end to end, and what rules I had to put in place to keep the result honest. That's Part 3.

References

  • SAP ADT REST API protocol notes verified against a live SAP BTP ABAP Cloud / S/4HANA Cloud system, recorded in this project's own docs (docs/sap-adt/)

entry.title: CDS Migration: Define View to Define View Entity
entry.content:
This article serves as a reference for migrating a classic CDS DDIC based view (Define View) to CDS view entity (Define View Entity). 
In this blog, I will demonstrate the complete practical migration process from a classic CDS Define View to a CDS View Entity. The article covers the migration analysis, pre-checks, post-checks, handling migration issues such as semantic annotations, performing the actual migration, and validating the migrated CDS View Entity.
The focus of this blog is not just on the theory, but on the hands-on steps and screenshots at each stage, making it easier to understand what happens during the migration and how to resolve the issues encountered along the way.

Difference between Define View and Define View entity 

Define View 

Define View entity 

  • ABAP 7.40 
  • Generated an additional ABAP DDIC SQL View (@AbapCatelog.SqlViewName) 
  • Several checks at runtime (Without annotation validation) 
  • Can migrate to define view entity 
  • This view is obsolete but still runs, no further new development 
  • ABAP 7.55 
  • No DDIC managed SQL view, generated directly as a SQL view on the database 
  • Static activation is Stricker (data types, annotations) 
  • Can’t migrate to define view (no self service) 
  • All new development used this entity 

Note: Nothing is migrated automatically. SAP explicit states that semantics can change during migration, so every view must be reviewed by a developer – there is no safe default migration path.

There are 2 ways to migrate Define View to Define View Entity: 

  • By using Classic Report Programs tool 
  • By using ADT migration wizard tool 

Practical Implementation demonstration

  • By Using ADT Migration wizard 

Example: Sales Order Define View

  • Here you can right click on Define View and observe the option to migrate the Define View to Define View entity 

  • It will prompt you to select CDS DDIC based view

  • Click on Next button - it will take us to the Select Migration options screen

  • Simulation -> Test First (Will this migration work without errors) 
    • Trial run / validation 
  • When you select Simulations: 
    • ADT analyzes the existing CDS' DDIC-based view.  
    • It checks whether the object can be migrated to a CDS View Entity.  
    • It detects potential migration errors or incompatibilities.  
    • It produces a migration log.  
    • No new CDS View Entity is created.  
    • The existing CDS view remains unchanged.  
    • It is safe to use during analysis/development. 
  • Migration -> Actual migration (Actual Create new CDS entity) 
    • Generates CDS entity as inactive objects, the activate manually 
  • When you select migration: 
    • ADT performs the actual migration.  
    • It generates the corresponding CDS View Entity.  
    • The generated CDS View Entity is initially inactive.  
    • You can review the generated source code.  
    • You can correct any issues manually.  
    • Then you activate the generated object.  
    • You should test the migrated object afterward. 
  • Select Simulation radio button -> Click on Next button -> Check the Simulation migration logs once after running

  • In the below picture, you can expand and check all the logs to see which objects were impacted by the migration, it also shows the status of each log entry 

  • Once you have completed the Simulation process, go back, select the Migration radio button, and click Next. It will then ask for transport request (TR), Select TR and click Finish. 
  • Before that try to resolve all the possible errors.
  • Mainly we get warnings and errors related to Currency, Units, Castings, where conditions.

  • Once the respective Semantics annotations are added for Net Amount and Order Quantity, the error will disappear automatically, 
  • So, in this way, we must resolve all the warnings and errors while raised during migration. 
  • If we execute the data view, we can see the same output

Note: Once a CDS DDIC – based Define view has been successfully migrated to a Define View Entity, it cannot be migrated back to its original view state. So be careful before migrating the view. 

By Using Classic Report Program tool

@AbapCatalog.sqlViewName: 'ZIDVPO' 
@AbapCatalog.compiler.compareFilter: true 
@AbapCatalog.preserveKey: true 
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED 
@EndUserText.label: 'Purchase Order Details' 
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true 

define view ZI_DV_PURORDER 
as select from ekko 
inner join ekpo on ekko.ebeln = ekpo.ebeln 
{ 
key ekko.ebeln as po, 
key ekpo.ebelp as poitem, 
ekko.bsart as potype, 
ekko.ekorg as poorg, 
ekko.ekgrp as pogrp, 
ekko.lifnr as supplier, 
ekpo.matnr as material, 
ekpo.werks as plant, 
ekpo.lgort as storagelocation, 
ekko.waers as currency, 
ekpo.menge as quantity, 
ekpo.meins as uom, 
ekpo.netwr as netvalue, 
ekpo.netpr as unitprice, 
ekpo.peinh as priceunit, 

case 
when ekpo.loekz = 'L' then 'DELETED' 
when ekpo.elikz = 'X' then 'DELIVERY COMPLETED' 
when ekpo.menge = 0 then 'NO QUANTITY' 
when ekpo.menge > 0 and ekpo.elikz <> 'X' then 'OPEN' 
else 'UNKNOWN' 
end as po_status, 

case 
when ekko.bsart = 'ZSUB' then 'SUBCONTRACTING' 
when ekko.bsart = 'NB' then 'STANDARD' 
when ekko.bsart = 'FO' then 'FRAMEWORK' 
else 'OTHER' 
end as po_type_description, 

case 
when ekpo.netwr >= 100000 then 'HIGH VALUE' 
when ekpo.netwr >= 50000 then 'MEDIUM VALUE' 
when ekpo.netwr > 0 then 'LOW VALUE' 
else 'NO VALUE' 
end as value_category, 

case 
when ekpo.menge >= 1000 then 'HIGH QUANTITY' 
when ekpo.menge >= 100 then 'MEDIUM QUANTITY' 
when ekpo.menge > 0 then 'LOW QUANTITY' 
else 'NO QUANTITY' 
end as quantity_category, 

case 
when ekpo.loekz = 'L' then 'CLOSED' 
when ekpo.elikz = 'X' and ekpo.erekz = 'X' then 'FULLY COMPLETED' 
when ekpo.elikz = 'X' and ekpo.erekz <> 'X' then 'DELIVERY COMPLETED - INVOICE PENDING' 
when ekpo.elikz <> 'X' and ekpo.erekz = 'X' then 'INVOICE COMPLETED - DELIVERY PENDING' 
when ekpo.menge > 0 and ekpo.netwr > 100000 and ekko.bsart = 'ZSUB' 
then 'HIGH VALUE SUBCONTRACTING PO' 
when ekpo.menge > 0 and ekpo.netwr > 100000 then 'HIGH VALUE OPEN PO' 
when ekpo.menge > 0 then 'NORMAL OPEN PO' 
else 'CHECK REQUIRED' 
end as business_status, 
ekko.aedat as creationdate 
} 
where ekko.bukrs = '1000'

Analysis: RUT_WHERE_USE_SQLVIEW  

  • List all usages of CDS managed DDIC views 

Analysis: RUTDDLS_MIGRATION_CANDIDATES 

  • In this phase we need the report RUTDDLS_MIGRATION_CANDIDATES to analyze the Core Data Services in the system that we want to migrate. If we run the report for the two views, we get an assessment of the migration possibility of the views. 
  • Run report to list every classic DEFINE VIEW in the system 

Implementation: RUTDDLSV2MIGRATION 

  • Main report for Mass migration. 
  • Select the DDLs source to migrate – directly by name, or by package, system, or user
  • Run in 'Simulate Generation' mode first. Review the protocol for errors and warnings without changing anything in the system. 

  • However, we now receive errors when implementing the objects. If we take a closer look at the protocol, we find the error message that the reference fields are not contained in the entity.  

    • Give DDL name in respective input field and click on F8 execute button 

  • Here we got error in Post Check logs 

Simulation Generation: 

  • In this mode, the tool does not perform the actual migration but provides a comprehensive analysis of the Classical CDS View. It checks for: 
  • Consistency: Ensures the CDS View follows the required structure.  
  • Errors: Flags with potential issues and inconsistencies.  
  • Pre-checks & Post-checks: Validates whether the CDS View adheres to migration standards before and after processing. 
  • Rule Processing: Provides insights into the underlying rules that will govern the migration. 

Just double-click on the error log to get the complete information. The error indicates that the reference information for the currency and quantity fields is missing. From this, we can understand that, for a CDS View Entity, we need to add the appropriate semantic annotations for amount/currency and quantity/unit fields.

  • In the screen below, observe the highlighted code carefully. It shows what needs to be added or which new features are introduced after migrating from a define view to a define view entity. 

  • Here, we have two options either migrate first and then add the required annotations or add the required annotations before starting the migration process. 

Now, select Generate Inactive Version radio button in Execution Mode, click on F8 Execute button 

This mode performs the actual migration, converting your Classical CDS View into a CDS View Entity. It generates the new version in an inactive state, allowing for post-migration testing and adjustments before activation. This ensures a smooth transition without disrupting ongoing operations. 

Enter the TR here and Click on Execute (F8)/

  • Go to, ADT refresh the Package or Project we can see the migrated entity

  • If we try to ACTIVATE with error will get an activation error like this 

  • Once added @Semantics.amount.currencyCode: 'Currency' annotation the activation done successfully. 

Why Migrate to CDS View Entities 

Migrating to CDS View Entities offers several key benefits:  

  • Improved Performance: CDS View Entities are optimized for better performance, particularly in SAP S/4HANA environments.  
  • Scalability: They allow for more flexible and scalable data models that can evolve with your business needs.  
  • Future-Proofing: The CDS View Entity model is the foundation for future SAP developments, especially for integration with Fiori and other modern SAP applications. 
  • Consistency and Integration: The migration enhances consistency across SAP systems and improves integration with advanced analytics and reporting tools. 

Conclusion: 

Migrating the old views to the new entities definitely makes sense, since a second object, the SQL view, is no longer necessary. The activation times for views will also increase significantly, which will speed up our working time.

entry.title: Mastering %tky in SAP RAP: Why RAP Prefers Technical Keys
entry.content:
Introduction:

If you have worked with Actions in the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP), you may have noticed %tky being used when passing instance keys in EML statements. At the same time, you may have come across several RAP examples where %key is used for a similar purpose.
This naturally raises an important question: Are %key and %tky the same? If not, what is the difference, and which one should we use?

The Lesson That Taught Me the Difference:
For a long time, I used %key out of habit because it looked cleaner. The turning point for me happened during a recent project where we took a standard, non-draft Billing application and enabled draft capability to improve the user experience.

Immediately after deploying the change, our custom action UpdateBillingDate started failing silently. Users would trigger the action on a draft screen, but the UI wouldn't update.

During a deep debugging session, I discovered why: %key only carries the business primary keys. When our action executed an EML MODIFY ENTITIES statement using %key, it completely stripped out the %is_draft flag. The RAP framework assumed we were trying to modify the active database table directly instead of the draft buffer, resulting in a silent failure. Switching the logic to %tky fixed the bug instantly. That debugging session made it clear that understanding this distinction is vital for transactional processing.

In this blog, we’ll take a closer look at %tky and %key, understand how they differ, see where each one is used, and explore why %tky is generally preferred when working with RAP instance processing. 

By the end of this blog, you’ll have a clear understanding of technical keys vs. semantic keys and why %tky plays such an important role in SAP RAP. 

A Quick Recap: BDEF Derived Types and % Components:

When working with RAP behavior implementations, the framework automatically provides BDEF derived types.

You will encounter these types in several places, for example:

  • MODIFY ENTITIES
  • READ ENTITIES
  • Action parameters
  • FAILED
  • REPORTED
  • RESULT

Each derived type contains: 

  • Entity fields - your CDS fields (Billed, Billdate, etc.) 
  • % components - system-generated fields prefixed with % 

Examples include: 

  • %key 
  • %tky 
  • %cid 
  • %control 
  • %is_draft 

These % components carry additional runtime information required by RAP during transactional processing. 

What Is %key? 

%key is a component group that contains the primary key fields of the entity. 

In our Billing Document example:

key-%key-BillId

is equivalent to:

key-BillId

So %key is simply a structured way to access all key fields together. 

It represents the business identity of an instance.

What Is %tky? 

%tky stands for transactional key. 

As per SAP documentation, it uniquely identifies a RAP BO instance within a transaction. 

Unlike %key, it is not limited to business keys.

It includes: 

  • %key → business key fields 
  • %is_draft → identifies draft vs active instance 
  • %pid→ used in late numbering scenarios 

 So conceptually: 

%tky = %key + %is_draft (+ %pid)

Even in non-draft scenarios, %tky is still present, the extra fields are just initial. 

Back to Our Action: UpdateBillingDate 

Let’s revisit the action implementation. 

METHOD updatebillingdate. 

  MODIFY ENTITIES OF zsan_i_bill_header IN LOCAL MODE 
     ENTITY zsan_i_bill_header 
     UPDATE FIELDS ( BillDate ) 
     WITH VALUE #( FOR key IN keys 
       ( %tky    = key-%tky 
         BillDate = key-%param-BillDate ) ) 
     FAILED   failed 
     REPORTED reported. 

  READ ENTITIES OF zsan_i_bill_header IN LOCAL MODE 
     ENTITY zsan_i_bill_header 
     ALL FIELDS 
     WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys ) 
     RESULT DATA(lt_bill_header). 

  result = VALUE #( FOR bill IN lt_bill_header 
     ( %tky   = bill-%tky 
       %param = bill ) ). 

ENDMETHOD.

Here, %tky is used in three places: 

  1. While updating records
  2. While reading data
  3. While building the result

At this point, replacing %tky with %key would still work, but only because draft is not enabled yet.

Where %key Can Become a Problem

Consider this simplified implementation:

MODIFY ENTITIES OF zsan_i_bill_header IN LOCAL MODE
  ENTITY zsan_i_bill_header
  UPDATE FIELDS ( BillDate )
  WITH VALUE #(
    FOR key IN keys
    (
      %key-BillId = key-%key-BillId
      BillDate    = key-%param-BillDate
    )
  ).

In a non-draft scenario, this may work perfectly.

There is only one relevant instance for:

BillId = 1001

But after enabling draft, the same business key may exist in both active and draft contexts.

Now the business key alone does not carry the complete transactional identity.

This is the key difference:

%key ↓ Business identity %tky ↓ Transactional identity

%tky vs %key

Differences 

%key 

%tky 

Contains 

Business key only 

Business + transactional info 

Draft support 

No 

Yes 

Late numbering 

Not reliable 

Supported 

failed/reported 

Limited 

Recommended 

Future-proof 

No 

Yes 

SAP guidance 

Legacy usage 

Preferred 

Why I Prefer %tky as the Default

After encountering this issue, I started treating %tky as my default choice whenever I am dealing with an existing RAP instance.

There are a few reasons for this.

1. It Is More Future-Proof

Today your application may not use draft.

Tomorrow it might.

If your code consistently works with %tky, you don't have to revisit every EML statement just because draft capability was introduced later.

For example:

%tky = key-%tky

already carries the transactional context.

That makes the code less dependent on whether the application currently happens to be draft-enabled.

2. It Fits RAP Transactional Processing

RAP is not simply about reading and updating database records.

It manages business object instances inside a transactional context.

That is an important distinction.

When performing operations such as:

MODIFY ENTITIES
READ ENTITIES

you are working with RAP's transactional model.

Using %tky makes that intention explicit.

3. It Is Important for FAILED and REPORTED

When reporting failures or messages, RAP needs to know which instance the message belongs to.

For example:

APPEND VALUE #(
  %tky = ls_billdoc-%tky
) TO failed-zsan_i_bill_header.

Using %tky allows the framework to associate the failure with the correct transactional instance.

This becomes especially important when multiple instances can have the same business key but belong to different transactional contexts.

4. It Supports Late Numbering Scenarios

Another important scenario is late numbering.

In such cases, the final business key may not yet be available at the point where RAP is processing the instance.

This is where transactional identification becomes particularly useful.

The transactional identity can use information such as %pid to keep track of the instance before the final key is assigned.

So, again:

Business key
    ↓
May not be available yet

Transactional identity
    ↓
Still available

That is another reason why %tky is more appropriate for transactional instance handling.

What About %cid?

There is one important distinction to remember.

When you are creating a new instance, the instance does not exist yet.

Therefore, you cannot use %tky in the same way as you would for an existing instance.

For create operations, %cid is commonly used as the client-generated temporary identifier.

For example:

%cid = 'CID_001'

This allows RAP to correlate the newly created instance and its subsequent processing.

So a simplified way to remember the identifiers is:

CREATE
   ↓
%cid

Existing instance / transactional processing
   ↓
%tky

A Simple Mental Model

If I had to explain %key and %tky to someone new to RAP, I would use this analogy.

Imagine a hotel.

The room number is your business key.

For example:

Room = 1001

But imagine that the hotel has two reservations associated with the same room in different contexts.

Knowing only:

1001

may not be enough to identify the exact transaction you are currently working with.

The transactional key gives the framework additional information to identify the correct instance in its current transactional context.

So:

%key
= "Which business object?"

%tky
= "Which transactional instance?"

This is not a formal definition, but I find it useful as a mental model when writing RAP code.

One Rule I Keep in Mind

For existing RAP instances, my general rule is:

Prefer %tky when the operation is about transactional instance identification.

%key is still useful when you specifically need the entity's business key—for example, when interacting with legacy logic, custom APIs, or interfaces that only understand the actual database/business keys.

And for create operations, %cid has its own role because the instance does not yet exist.

 Conclusion:
In my daily development workflow, %tky has become my default choice for all EML operations, validations, and determinations. The only edge case where I intentionally reach for %key is when I need to interface with legacy, custom APIs or older RFC function modules that only understand plain business keys. Beyond that, sticking to %tky saves hours of troubleshooting and keeps your codebase inherently scalable.

entry.title: ABAP AI's Three Circles in Practice
entry.content:
ABAP AI's Three Circles in Practice (Series 3, Part 5: Clean Core + AI)

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 5 of 6 | Published September 2026

TL;DR: SAP frames ABAP AI as three concentric circles — ABAP Cloud core, developer AI tooling, and agents — and says they "coexist and reinforce each other." That's easy to nod along to and hard to picture. This part walks the consolidation case from Part 4 back through all three circles, showing where an agent did the finding, where AI tooling did the building, and where a human still had to make the one call none of it could make for her.

The model, in Liénard's own framing

In an August 2026 interview with SAP News, Sonja Liénard — SVP and head of ABAP platform, and head of ABAP AI — laid out the vision she uses internally:

"ABAP Cloud is at the center, as the modern, clean-core variant of our language for long-term stability. The second circle is the ABAP AI layer: developer tools for code explanation, code generation, and ghost texting. The outer circle is comprised of AI agents, a network of specialized agents for complex and multi-step tasks such as transformation, migration, and quality validation."

Three layers, one direction of travel: stable core, assisted authoring, autonomous orchestration. Liénard's own qualifier is the part worth sitting with — "the circles coexist and reinforce each other." Not replace. Reinforce. The rest of this piece is what that actually looks like on a real object, not a slide.

The case: back to the three Z-programs

Part 4 left off with a decision, not just a diagram. Three Z-programs — same domain, inconsistent parameter names, duplicated logic — got consolidated into one CAP service: one entity, one function branching internally on method, properly typed. That decision didn't happen in one circle. It happened across all three, in sequence.

Outer circle — an agent found the debt.


Part 2 of this series covered ATC as clean core's quality gate — SAP Note 3565942, the Kernseife extensibility checks, the Clean Core Levels A–D. What Part 2 didn't cover is that a human doesn't have to run that assessment manually anymore. SAP's Mass Clean Core Adoption Agent, announced alongside the custom code migration agent this year, scans exactly this kind of landscape: it identifies clean-core ATC violations, fixes what it can fix outright, and — for anything that needs judgment — returns a structured recommendation instead of guessing. Three Z-programs with overlapping logic and no released-API path is precisely the "needs judgment" case. The agent's output wasn't "here's your new service." It was "here are three violations that look related — a human should look at this together."

That's the outer circle doing what Liénard describes it doing: multi-step, structured, but explicitly handing off the decision it isn't built to make.

The decision itself — nobody's circle.


Consolidating three programs into one service, choosing the entity shape, deciding what the function's internal branching should look like — that's architecture. None of the three circles claims to do this, and SAP doesn't pretend otherwise. Liénard's own framing of what AI frees up is "decisions regarding business logic and architecture, as well as verifying quality." The agent's flag started the process; a person's judgment shaped the service.

Middle circle — AI tooling built it.


Once the shape was decided, the actual writing is where the second circle earns its place. Two capabilities do the heavy lifting here, both shipped as part of Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities: code explanation and ghost text (SAP's term for inline, accept-as-you-type code generation). Code explanation is what makes it safe to consolidate in the first place — before merging three programs, you need to actually understand what each one's edge cases were doing, not just what they were named. Ghost text is what makes writing the consolidated version fast rather than tedious: typed intent, generated implementation, still reviewed line by line before it ships. SAP's own design principle for these tools, stated in their Sapphire 2026 announcement, is to explain and understand existing code before proposing changes — protecting the investment already made in the custom code, not just replacing it wholesale.

Center circle — where it had to land.


The consolidated service is only worth building if it lives somewhere stable. That's the center circle's job, and it's the one that doesn't get a dramatic moment — ABAP Cloud is the boring, load-bearing constraint that made everything upstream of it accountable to something. The service consumes released APIs, not internal tables. It sits inside the debt register from Part 4, not outside it. If the core weren't clean to begin with, there'd be nothing stable for the agent to scan or the tooling to generate against — this is the part Part 1 of this series argued from the other direction.

What the roadmap says about where this is headed

This isn't a one-off case study; it's the current shape of a fast-moving roadmap. As of Q2 2026, the ABAP MCP server shipped for both Eclipse and VS Code, opening agentic ABAP development to any MCP-compatible client — this is what Part 3 walked through directly with the Custom Code Migration Agent. Alongside the migration agent, SAP shipped the Mass Clean Core Adoption Agent used above and a Web Dynpro-to-Fiori modernization agent for a different class of legacy debt. A second agent, focused specifically on clean-core transformation, is planned for Q3 2026, with continued work on multi-agent orchestration through the rest of the year. SAP's own early evaluations target a 40% efficiency gain in custom code transformation work — a number worth watching for independent validation as more of these agents reach general availability, not taking at face value yet.

The honest gap in the model

The three-circles diagram implies clean handoffs — agent flags, tooling builds, core absorbs. The real sequence had a fourth step wedged in the middle that belongs to none of the circles: a person deciding what "consolidated" should actually mean for this domain. SAP's framing accounts for this implicitly — Liénard's answer about what AI frees up isan admission that architecture and business logic decisions stay human. But it's worth saying plainly, because it's the difference between "agents do clean core" and what's actually happening, which is closer to: agents surface the debt, tooling removes the friction of fixing it, and the core stays the one thing that has to be true before either of the other two circles means anything.

Part 6 closes this series by tying that center circle to something more concrete than "stable" — how a clean core is what makes agent governance actually enforceable, through the MCP Gateway and AI Agent Hub verification, rather than a compliance slide.

If you've run an agent-assisted clean-core assessment on your own landscape: did the agent's flag match where your own architects would have looked first, or did it surface something you'd have missed?

entry.title: How to Create an RAP Based Custom UI5 App and Deploy it to SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud
entry.content:
Image/data in this blog is from SAP internal systems, sample data, or demo systems. Any resemblance to real data is purely coincidental.

Do you want to build a custom SAPUI5/Fiori application on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) and make it available as a tile in the SAP Fiori Launchpad?

This blog walks you through the complete end-to-end process — from creating the RAP-based OData service in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, developing a Fiori Elements List Report application in SAP Business Application Studio (BAS), deploying the application to SAP S/4HANA Cloud, and finally configuring the required IAM objects to make the application available as a tile in the Fiori Launchpad.

The complete flow covered in this blog is:

RAP Backend → OData Service → Fiori Elements Application → Deployment → IAM Configuration → Business Role → Fiori Launchpad

Overview: SAP Fiori Element Applications in the ABAP Environment

The above diagram illustrates that a UI developer implements the SAP Fiori application against the OData service and defines the tile as part of the application. Once this is done, the developer deploys the SAP Fiori application to the SAPUI5 ABAP repository in the development tenant.

An administrator provides access to the OData service and the tile via a business role.

A business user that is assigned to the business role can access the tile from SAP Fiori launchpad and launch the application.

Generating and Deploying Your Application

Before generating and deploying the application, ensure that the following prerequisites are met:

​Prerequisites

  • Need to create development package in ABAP Development Tools for Eclipse. See Creating ABAP Packages.
  • Need to expose a RAP business service as an OData service. See Using Service Binding Editor for OData V2 Service.
  • Business catalog SAP_A4C_BC_DEV_UID_PC is assigned to your user, which allows you to discover available OData services and deploy your application.
  • Business catalog SAP_CORE_BC_EXT_TST is assigned to your user, which allows you to preview your application. See Generate Deployment Configuration ABAP.
  • You have an open transport request.

With the prerequisites in place, let's proceed step by step to create and deploy a RAP-based custom SAPUI5 application in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

Step 1: Create RAP business service as an OData service using ADT.

Flow : Development Package -> Data Definition -> Service Definition -> Service Binding (RAP business service as an OData service)

  1. Open ADT and connect to development tenant
  2. Create Development package
  3. Create Data Definition
  4. Create Service Definition -> Reference Object ->Click on Browse -> Search and Select Standard data source (Example: I_PURCHASEORDERAPI01)
  5. Create Service Binding

     

Step 2: Generating and Deploying RAP Based Custom UI5 Application.

  1. Open Business Application Studio via BTP Cockpit 
  2. BAS is accessed through the SAP BTP Cockpit — not through the S/4HANA Fiori Launchpad. Open BTP Cockpit → Subaccount → Instances and Subscriptions.
  3. Launch the SAP Business Application Studio and Create a New Dev Space
  4. Select SAP Fiori -> Create Dev Space -> Open the Dev Space
  5. Create Project from Template
  6. Select SAP Fiori Generator -> List Report Page -> Select the System as "Development tenant -> Service as "Service Binding created using the ADT"
  7. Select Entity set and Table type as "Responsive".
  8. Fill all the Project Attributes.
  9. Define the "Deployment Configuration" ->Create the SAPUI5 ABAP Repository (name should have prefix as Z*)
  10. Define the Fiori Launchpad Configuration.
  11. Click on Finish.
  12. Click on Preview Application and test the application.
  13. Click on Deploy.
  14. Check the Terminal message shown as "Deployment Successful" .

Step 3: Testing RAP-Based Application in S/4HANA Public Cloud

Deployed a RAP-based application in the SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud system, However, while testing the application, I encountered an authorization issue when trying to consume the service in the SAP Fiori app.

How to handle Authorization Issues During UI Preview

  1. Create IAM App using ADT

     

  2. Check the BSP Library and Fiori User Interface (Which is auto generated once the application deployed successfully)
  3. Assign the "Fiori Launchpad App Descr Item ID" to IAM App.
  4. Publish Locally.
  5. Create Business Catalog and assign the IAM App.
  6. Publish Locally.
  7. Launch the Fiori Launchpad (S/4HANA Public Cloud Development System).
  8. Create the Business Role using the "Maintain Business Role" App.
  9. Assign the Business catalog and Business user to a Business Role.
  10. Try accessing the RAP Based Custom UI5 Application.

Summary:

In this blog, we explored the complete end-to-end process of building and deploying a RAP-based custom SAPUI5/Fiori application in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

Starting with the creation of a RAP business service in ABAP Development Tools (ADT), we exposed the business data as an OData service and consumed it in a Fiori Elements List Report application generated in SAP Business Application Studio (BAS). We then deployed the application to the SAPUI5 ABAP Repository in the SAP S/4HANA Cloud development tenant and verified the successful deployment.

We also covered the authorization and launchpad integration aspects by creating the required IAM App and Business Catalog, assigning them to a Business Role, and making the application available as a tile in the SAP Fiori Launchpad. This final step ensures that business users can securely access the application through role-based authorizations.

Conclusion:

The combination of the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP), SAP Fiori Elements, and SAP Business Application Studio provides a streamlined approach for developing enterprise applications on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

By following the steps outlined in this blog, you can build a custom application, deploy it to the SAP S/4HANA Cloud environment, integrate it with the SAP Identity and Access Management (IAM) framework, and expose it through the SAP Fiori Launchpad. Understanding the complete flow—from backend service creation to frontend deployment and authorization setup—helps accelerate custom application development while ensuring a secure and consistent user experience.

I hope this blog helps you get started with RAP-based application development and deployment in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Feel free to share your feedback, questions, or experiences in the comments section.

  • 3399748 - You do not have start authorization for R3TR IWSV XXXXXXXXXX 0001, return code4 - Developer Extensibility - SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition - SAP for Me

entry.title: SAP Business Application Studio Integration with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
entry.content:
Introduction:

SAP Business Application Studio (BAS) is a development environment that provides the tools required to build SAP Fiori and SAPUI5 applications.

When developing custom applications for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, SAP Business Application Studio can be integrated with the SAP S/4HANA Cloud tenant to enable developers to access the required services and use them during application development.

This blog provides a step-by-step guide to setting up the integration between SAP Business Application Studio and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

The setup covers the required trust configuration, SAP Business Application Studio setup, connectivity between BAS and the SAP S/4HANA Cloud tenant, and creation of a Dev Space for SAP Fiori application development.

The steps described in this blog are based on the SAP documentation:

The integration setup consists of the following steps:

SAP Cloud Identity Services
↓
SAP BTP Subaccount
↓
SAP Business Application Studio
↓
SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition Tenant
↓
SAP Fiori Dev Space

In this blog, we will cover the following topics:

  • Set Up Trust Between SAP Cloud Identity Services and SAP BTP Subaccount (Set the "Subject Identifier Name" in Step 5 to "Email")
  • Set Up SAP Business Application Studio for Development
  • Connect SAP Business Application Studio and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Tenant
  • Create a Dev Space for SAP Fiori Apps

Step 1: Set Up Trust Between SAP Cloud Identity Services and SAP BTP Subaccount

The first step is to establish trust between SAP Cloud Identity Services and the SAP BTP subaccount.

This trust configuration enables users to authenticate when accessing applications and services in the SAP BTP environment.

Navigate to the relevant SAP BTP subaccount and open the Security → Trust Configuration section.

Configure the required trust relationship with SAP Cloud Identity Services according to your landscape.

Refer to Set Up Trust Between SAP Cloud Identity Services and SAP BTP Subaccount (Set the "Subject Identifier Name" in Step 5 to "Email")

Step 2: Set Up SAP Business Application Studio for Development

After establishing the trust configuration, the next step is to set up SAP Business Application Studio in the SAP BTP subaccount.

SAP Business Application Studio is provided as a service in SAP BTP and must be subscribed to before it can be used for application development.

Refer to Set Up SAP Business Application Studio for Development
